title: Battery News Headlines
content:
Battery News
Waymo's Santa Monica charging stations halted; Factorial and SK On advance solid-state battery manufacturing; Altilium patents EcoCathode recycling; Ferrari's Luce EV excels in China; and iPhone's Emergency Override risks damage; and more.
July 30, 2026
5 Min Read
Credit: Rifqyhsn, Hordieiev Roman / iStock / Getty Images Plus via Getty Images
The battery industry moves at a fast pace: The articles
Battery Technology
publishes represent only a fraction of what’s happening in this quickly evolving industry. That’s the idea behind this curated and regularly updated digest of links to breaking news related to the battery and energy storage industry. Some of these stories may become the subject of analysis by our own team—but we’re sharing them here, unfiltered, so that you can get them on your radar right away.
To keep the stream fresh, we will update this digest regularly—so please check back often!
In a rush? Watch the 60-second news summary of the previous week in the YouTube video below. Scroll down for the full coverage.
A judge ordered Waymo to halt overnight use of two Santa Monica
EV charging stations
after residents complained of noise, light, and traffic disturbances from operations.
(LATimes)
Waymo vehicle in San Francisco. Courtesy of Justin Sullivan/Getty Images News.
Factorial and SK On signed an MoU to explore
solid-state battery manufacturing
, combining advanced technology with global manufacturing expertise to accelerate industrialization and scalability.
(Factorial)
Altilium secures UK patent for EcoCathode, an innovative hydrometallurgical process
recycling lithium-ion batteries
, enabling sustainable recovery of high-purity cathode materials for domestic EV battery production.
(Altilium)
The 2027 Ferrari Luce is the company's first battery-electric vehicle. Courtesy of Ferrari.
Ferrari's Luce EV
hit its 2026 sales target of 500 units
within two months, driven by strong demand in China despite polarizing design reviews.
(Reuters)
Emergency Override charging bypasses iPhone's liquid detection, risking
charging port corrosion
or short-circuiting. Use only in emergencies, ensuring no liquid is present to avoid damage.
Earlier:
CATL exhibition display, Frankfurt Auto Show. Credit: Sean Gallup / Getty Images News via Getty Images
The world’s largest battery maker, CATL,
reported sharply higher profit in the first half of 2026
as booming demand for energy-storage systems and resilient electric-vehicle battery sales offset weakening appetite for EVs in China. Net profit surged 42% from a year earlier; revenue increased 55%. (
Wall Street Journal
New data released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reveal growth of more than 10% in electrical generation by renewable energy sources in the first five months of 2026. Moreover, solar, wind and battery storage are projected to add about 83.0 gigawatts (GW) of new generating capacity in the US by May 31, 2027. EIA foresees
battery energy storage adding another 23,241.1 MW by June 1, 2027 – an increase of almost 48%
, bringing the total up to 72,002.0 MW. (
Renewables Now

24% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, up from 22% in 2Q25

Tesla’s Q2 sales bounced back after large stretches of last year went sideways, landing the company a record quarter. Then
Wednesday’s Q2 earnings landed
with a thud. By Thursday’s close,
shares had slid 14.5%, wiping out $214.5 billion of market value in one session
—the worst single day in Tesla’s history, and the sum lost exceeds the entire current market cap of every other automaker. (
Carscoops
Credit: Alexander Sikov / iStock via Getty Images
LG Energy Solution has filed a patent infringement lawsuit against Chinese battery maker EVE Energy
in the United States. The litigation involves five patents, including four related to cylindrical batteries and one covering battery separators. The disputed portfolio includes patents related to tabless technology for cylindrical batteries. (
The Elec
Earlier:
A US Senate panel advanced the Connected Vehicle Security Act, potentially
banning Mercedes-Benz sales
due to Chinese ownership exceeding 15%, sparking debate over national security risks.
(Bloomberg)
The 2026 Mercedes-Benz VLE electric van. Courtesy of Mercedes-Benz.
LG Energy Solution and GM will
restart Ohio's Ultium Cells battery plant

(The Korea Herald)
A Cirba Solutions study reveals
US battery recycling

(InnovationNewsNetwork)
Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra offers a 5,000 mAh battery with a slimmer foldable design. Courtesy of Samsung.
Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 series features
silicon-carbon batteries

(Techradar)

title: Factorial and SK On to cooperate on solid-state batteries - electrive.com
content:
Solid-state battery developer Factorial Energy and South Korean battery giant SK On are advancing the commercialisation of solid-state cells. A newly agreed partnership will examine how existing production structures can be used for the next generation of cells.
Mercedes is already testing Factorial's technology
Image: Mercedes-Benz
The newly-formed strategic partnership between solid-state battery specialist Factorial and global battery manufacturer SK On aims to accelerate the market launch of its FEST technology, which is currently being tested in real-world applications, including with the
Stellantis brand Dodge
. The two companies have signed a memorandum of understanding to jointly evaluate the technical feasibility and integration of solid-state cells into SK On’s existing lithium-ion production lines. The focus is on leveraging the South Korean group’s global manufacturing capabilities to scale Factorial’s FEST technology industrially.
SK On has an annual production capacity of over 200 gigawatt-hours worldwide and operates significant manufacturing facilities not only in South Korea but also in the USA. The cell manufacturer’s established automotive customers include major groups such as the Hyundai Motor Group, Ford, Volkswagen and Ferrari. Through this collaboration, Factorial aims to adopt a capital-efficient approach to industrialisation and utilise existing industrial infrastructure.
In a statement, Factorial founder and CEO Siyu Huang emphasised:”A battery breakthrough only matters if it can be manufactured at scale”. And, indeed, SK On’s global production facilities and expertise are crucial for integrating solid-state technology into global production ecosystems. The agreement highlights Factorial’s strategy of minimising the time and financial investment required for factory construction by collaborating with established industry leaders.
SK On also views the joint initiative as an important step in exploring future energy storage generations. “This collaboration provides an opportunity to evaluate the technical feasibility and manufacturing readiness of solid-state battery technologies, drawing on SK On’s battery technology and manufacturing expertise,” explains Ki-soo Park, Head of the Institute for Future Technology at SK On. The company will continue to actively seek opportunities to support innovative approaches in the next generation of energy storage solutions.
Factorial has been collaborating with various heavyweights in the global automotive industry for some time. The company’s strategic investors and partners include Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis. Real-world road tests with modified test vehicles have already been conducted with Mercedes-Benz, while Stellantis has successfully integrated high-energy cells into the aforementioned Dodge demonstration vehicle.
Additionally, the company is now being
supported by IQT
, a government-backed investor funded by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and acting on behalf of other US agencies. The goal is to rapidly make dual-use technologies available to government authorities. Solid-state batteries could, for example, power the energy demands of AI data centres or be deployed in drones. “The ability of Factorial’s solid-state batteries to deliver high power and operate in low temperature environments makes them very attractive for use in high-altitude or high-latitude applications,” said IQT manager Brian Smith regarding the investment. “We are delighted to be able to help the company accelerate and expand its footprint into the drone, UAV, and mobile robotics market.”

title: EU ‘Battery Booster’ funding applications now open - electrive.com
content:
The EU Commission has published a call for proposals to receive interest-free loans of up to €1.5 billion to support battery cell production projects.
Battery cell production at PowerCo (symbolic image)
Image: PowerCo
In June, the European Commission approved the
‘Battery Booster Facility’
following an
earlier delay
. The funding call has now been published, with applications open until 30 September 2026.
Under the programme, interest-free loans totalling up to €1.5 billion will be made available to support projects for battery cell production across the European Economic Area (EEA).
Projects must focus on producing battery cells suitable for use in electric vehicles. Additionally, at the time of application, projects must be in the start-up phase, represent the applicant’s first global large-scale commercial battery cell production initiative for electric vehicles, and have a planned annual production capacity of at least 10 gigawatt-hours.
Successful applicants can receive interest-free loans covering up to 60 per cent of eligible costs, with a maximum of €500 million per project. Given the highly specific requirements, the cell factories currently being ramped up by
(backed by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and TotalEnergies),
(among others, Renault), and
(VW Group) are likely to qualify.

title: 25 Examples of the History and Future of Electric Flight
content:
Industry Outlook
Automotive & Mobility
EVs and energy-storage get the most attention—but the aerospace industry is a growing locus for battery technology as electric airplanes, drones, and eVTOLs take wing. Here's a quick history.
July 30, 2026

Joby eVTOL
As we reported this week: At the Farnborough International Airshow, GE Aerospace, in collaboration with NASA, BETA Technologies, and Boeing, achieved a historic milestone by conducting
the first hybrid-electric flight above 30,000 feet
. In our June Editors Roundable, we discussed the US DoD Drone Dominance Program
completing its first major order cycle
, with 30,000 drones purchased and a stated goal of fielding more than 200,000 low-cost, battery-powered drones by 2027. It seems like a good time to update our look at major landmarks in the continuing history of electric flight (first detailed by former senior editor Kevin Clemons in 2021).
It’s hard to believe, but electrically powered flight has been around for 143 years. Lighter-than-air dirigibles in the 1880s were the first to use electric motors for propulsion and control, but it wasn’t until more recently that lithium-ion battery technology has allowed heavier-than-air electric aviation to prosper.
Here are 25 examples of how electric aviation started, progressed, and even where it may be headed in the future. These are only a few examples, almost every week a new start-up announces how it will change the world, how we travel, commute, and enjoy our recreation. Our advice: Hold on tight, it’s going to be a fun ride.

title: Electric Aviation Progress with Hybrid and Fully Electric Systems
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Battery Applications
Industry Trends
Recent advancements in electric aviation are boosting hybrid-electric propulsion systems and fully electric aircraft, thereby driving sustainability.
July 29, 2026
3 Min Read
Pilots from GE Aerospace and BETA Technologies supported flight tests in the US.
Courtesy of GE Aerospace.
electric aviation industry
continues to make significant strides, with recent developments showcasing advancements in hybrid-electric propulsion systems and fully electric aircraft. These milestones highlight the sector’s commitment to reducing emissions and enhancing efficiency, paving the way for a more sustainable future in aviation.
Hybrid electric flight reaches commercial heights
At the Farnborough International Airshow,
GE Aerospace
, in collaboration with NASA, BETA Technologies, and Boeing, achieved a historic milestone by conducting the first hybrid-electric flight above 30,000 feet. The system consists of a modified Saab 340B that includes GE Aerospace-developed motor/generators, power converters and inverters, controllers, Avio Aero gearboxes, Dowty propellers, Unison heat exchangers, torque sensing, and engine harnesses, and a CT7 engine.
The system, developed under NASA’s Electrified Powertrain Flight Demonstration (EPFD) project, powered the aircraft for a record-breaking two-hour hybrid-electric flight. H. Lawrence Culp, Jr., Chairman and CEO of GE Aerospace, emphasized the significance of this achievement, “The aviation industry’s first high-altitude hybrid electric flight is one for the history books. GE Aerospace is grateful to NASA, BETA Technologies, and Boeing for their collaborative partnership to accelerate hybrid electric technology to meet customer needs for greater efficiency, durability, and range.”
Related:
Range Rover GT Debuts as Electric Fastback With Off-Road Capability and Minimalist Interior
The hybrid system combines electric power with a traditional gas turbine, optimizing power management during different flight phases. BAE Systems provided advanced lithium-ion batteries, which played a critical role in powering the propeller and generating energy to recharge during flight. At the same time, Boeing subsidiary Aurora Flight Sciences supplied the complete nacelle.
BAE Systems' advanced battery system powered the first flight test of GE Aerospace's hybrid-electric propulsion demonstrator aircraft. Courtesy of BAE Systems.
BAE Systems’ Role in Hybrid-Electric Innovation
BAE Systems has emerged as a key player in advancing hybrid-electric aviation, providing the battery energy storage system for GE Aerospace’s hybrid-electric propulsion demonstrator. The system features advanced lithium-ion batteries and a safety-critical battery management system, enabling high power output without adding significant weight to the aircraft.
Trudy Palmer, Director of Airborne Power Systems at BAE Systems, highlighted the company’s contribution: “Our expertise in advanced battery technology and safety-critical battery management system design was crucial to enabling GE Aerospace to achieve this landmark moment. We are incredibly proud to be contributing to a more sustainable future for air travel.”
Related:
7 Battery-Powered Machines Transforming Construction & Mining Sites
The successful flight test at Farnborough marks a significant step toward commercializing hybrid-electric propulsion systems for narrow-body aircraft. BAE Systems and GE Aerospace plan to continue refining the system as they work toward achieving aviation certification.
Dovetail’s fully electric Cessna Caravan
In another significant development,
Dovetail Electric Aviation
announced a partnership with Norway’s Ludens Aviation to retrofit Cessna Caravans with fully electric propulsion systems. The retrofitted aircraft will feature Dovetail’s proprietary DovePack battery system and DovePower propulsion technology, designed to replace conventional turboprop engines with quieter, lower-emission alternatives.
Ludens Aviation plans to deploy the electric Caravans for skydiving operations in Norway, a market well-suited for sustainable aviation due to its short-cycle mission profiles. Kjetil Kriken, CEO of Ludens Aviation, highlighted the alignment between electric aircraft and skydiving: “Electric aircraft and skydiving are a perfect match: short cycles, fixed patterns above the same field, and a community that cares about noise and emissions.”
Related:
Navigating the Hybrid Shift
These developments underscore the remarkable progress in electric aviation, with hybrid and fully electric technologies offering promising solutions for a more sustainable future in air travel.

title: Avetta: US Organisations Unprepared for Supply Chain Risk
content:
Avetta: US Organisations Unprepared for Supply Chain Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
There is a growing gap between increasing supply chain risk and organisational response readiness. Credit: Getty
As disruption remains a constant risk to global supply chains, Avetta finds that organisations are left vulnerable due to poor visibility and response gaps
In today's world, work readiness is critical in order to stay resilient amid ongoing turbulence. Despite this understanding, however, many organisations are falling behind — knowing they are underprepared to deal with volatility, but unable to anticipate it.
Avetta has conducted a study exploring the preparedness of global organisations when dealing with risk, finding an increasing gap between risk and response.
The study reveals that a significant number of organisations are still relying on fragmented systems and
poor visibility
, unable to move beyond the reactive stage.
Compliance will always matter, but compliance alone doesn’t necessarily create readiness.
Abid Yousuf, Chief Customer Officer at Avetta
Increasing demands
As this era is seemingly defined by one major event after another, organisations around the world have had to adapt. Though the supply chain was once about cost savings and efficiency, it is now prioritising resilience and flexibility.
Demand is increasing, with a growing population and more global trade than ever before. With this, however, comes an increase in complexity. Manual processes are now no longer usable in the modern supply chain, instead, leaders rely on modern technology and AI agents in order to constantly monitor across the supply chain.
Despite this, some organisations are still falling behind in the readiness race, unable to correctly apply these new tools in order to remain operational in the face of turbulence.
Avetta, a leader in intelligent work readiness across global supply chains, conducted a survey to explore how organisations are responding to risk. In the survey, 500 US-based senior leaders across
supply chain, procurement
, operations and environmental health and safety explored their own operations. The survey revealed that, despite the awareness of
increasing risk complexity
, many organisations are unable to respond to that risk confidently.
"Supply chains are operating in a more volatile environment than ever, yet many organisations still lack a complete picture of the risks developing across their extended workforce and supplier networks," explains Abid Yousuf, Chief Customer Officer at Avetta, to Supply Chain Digital.
Abid Yousuf, Chief Customer Officer at Avetta. Credit: Avetta
"The companies that will outperform are those that turn fragmented data into actionable insight, giving teams the confidence to anticipate challenges and stay ahead of disruption."
Limited visibility
Though risk is increasing, organisations are still using disconnected systems, without full visibility or predictive capabilities. In order to better respond to these events, leaders need the capability to spot risk sooner. This will ensure safe and efficient operations, which can
protect the integrity
of the supply chain.
Within the survey, 77% of respondents report an increase in global supply chain and workforce risk over the past year, but only 44% have embedded real-time visibility into their operations. Their lack of centralisation and compliance risk factors means that many organisations are unable to respond to these growing risks. As a result, 68% of organisations underwent shutdowns or operational delays in the same 12 months.
Due to a lack of real-time visibility, 56% rely on visibility information which is manual, fragmented or delayed. This means that 39% identify risk only shortly before or after it has affected operations. Overall, 38% of respondents cite limited visibility into third-party risk as a barrier to effective risk mitigation.
Key facts
71% of respondents say compliance requirements have become more complex
More than half say compliance demands take time and resources away from other work
48% of respondents put real-time monitoring and predictive analytics as a core priority for strengthening risk response
Businesses need to tackle issues of data fragmentation. Credit: Getty
Another barrier to effective responsiveness is the compliance requirements themselves. Amid ongoing market shifts, compliance requirements have become more complex, with 42% of respondents saying this has created a barrier to
effective risk response
. Despite this, some leaders (24%) say they are unable to adjust to these needs because they rely on fragmented and manual processes.
"Compliance will always matter, but compliance alone doesn’t necessarily create readiness,” explains Abid.
“The organisations making the greatest progress are treating compliance as one part of a broader strategy that brings safety, supplier performance and operational risk together instead of managing them in silos.”
There is an operational gap of AI implementation. Credit: Getty
Investments into resilience
Organisations are increasingly investing in readiness, through emerging technologies and AI. Though an initial large-cost, when applied correctly, this technology can result in long-term cost savings and supply chain resilience.
Although most businesses (97.2%) are using AI within their
supply chain risk
management lifecycle, it is not applied across the entirety of their operations, with only 38% saying they have it fully embedded. Approximately half of respondents are using AI in a limited capacity, while 11% are still in the early stages of implementation.
Across respondents, AI is being used for:
Supplier analysis (55%)
Regulatory tracking (51%)
Compliance measurement (50%)
Predictive safety monitoring (46%)
Job safety analysis (42%).
As organisations are prioritising AI use for individual tasks, rather than organisation-wide transformation, they are leaving significant gaps in operational readiness.
Though organisations cannot eliminate uncertainty, they can prepare for it. As such, organisations are investing into opportunities to anticipate risk, such as gaining greater visibility into third-party safety, sustainability and financial risk.
“The next generation of supply chain leaders won’t be defined by how quickly they respond after a disruption occurs,” Abid adds. “They’ll be defined by how well they anticipate risk, align stakeholders and keep work moving forward before disruptions take hold. That’s what true readiness makes possible.”
The fragmentation is putting organisations at risk, but there is a growing awareness that stronger visibility could be the driver of resilience.

title: JLR: Increasing Circularity in Automotive Supply Chains
content:
JLR: Increasing Circularity in Automotive Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
JLR is increasing circularity across its supply chain and aiding higher transparency expectations by supporting international coalition ResponsibleGlass
Modern manufacturing produces 95m tonnes of CO₂ annually from glass alone, according to ResponsibleGlass. The material appears in buildings, vehicles, solar panels and advanced technologies but lacks unified
sustainability frameworks
for emission monitoring and mitigation across its value chain.
ResponsibleGlass was established in 2025 as a not-for-profit organisation to create a common global framework for glass production. The programme brings together raw material suppliers, manufacturers, brands, automotive companies, construction firms, recycling operators, architects, specifiers and civil society organisations.
The initiative has 23 founding members and supporters representing more than 150,000 employees and approximately US$90bn in annual revenue.
Members include JLR
, ARUP, Climate Group, DSS, WE Soda and ERM CVS.
"Glass is fundamental to modern life, from buildings and vehicles to solar technology and packaging, yet the sector has never operated under a unified, independent global sustainability framework," says Francis Sullivan, Chair of ResponsibleGlass.
JLR Reimagine - Our roadmap
Transparent sourcing across value chains
ResponsibleGlass has released its first draft standard incorporating six core ideas. Responsible sourcing requires companies to understand and assess the environmental and social impacts of raw materials, recycled materials and energy sources used in glass manufacturing.
The framework promotes supply chain transparency from silica sand and soda ash through to recovered glass and energy inputs. Management systems aim to ensure companies have the policies and reporting systems needed to manage sustainability performance.
Responsible business practice includes legal compliance, anti-corruption measures, stakeholder engagement, transparency and public reporting of sustainability data. Regulations like the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive are pushing companies to back up claims with verified data rather than self-reporting.
"The publication of this first ResponsibleGlass Draft Standard is an important milestone in changing that," says Francis.
Francis Sullivan is Chair of Responsible Glass and the former Head of Sustainability at HSBC
Upstream materials and downstream impact
Environmental performance covers GHG emissions, energy use, water stewardship, biodiversity, waste management, air emissions and pollution. Companies will be expected to measure, manage and disclose performance against key sustainability metrics.
People and communities involve worker health and safety, labour and human rights and engagement with local communities. Circularity and sustainable design encourage the use of recycled materials, improved recycling and recovery rates and the development of glass products designed to reduce environmental impacts.
"Every piece of glass is only as sustainable as the raw materials that go into it," says Alan Knight, Chief Sustainability Officer at WE Soda, the world's largest producer of soda ash, a key component of glassmaking.
"We've always believed that responsible sourcing upstream matters just as much as what happens downstream," says Alan.
Alan Knight, Chief Sustainability Officer at WE Soda
Natural materials in production chains
Natural soda ash has a lower carbon and water footprint than synthetic alternatives, according to Knight. The material is a critical component for glass and its sustainability credentials must be considered within a global standard.
"A global standard is a credible way for those credentials to be valued by the whole supply chain, right down to the end user," says Alan. "We were glad to be a founding member of ResponsibleGlass and this first draft is an important milestone for the glass industry."
ResponsibleGlass brings together the entire value chain from raw material producers and glassmakers to customers, sustainability experts and civil society organisations to develop a shared definition of responsible glassmaking. Sullivan says a standard is only as strong as the consensus behind it.
"But a standard is only as strong as the consensus behind it, which is why we're now inviting the wider industry, customers, policymakers and civil society to help us build a trusted global benchmark for responsible glassmaking," adds Francis. The organisation aims to create a trusted benchmark that accelerates progress on sustainability, enhances transparency and helps maximise the positive contribution glass can make to a more sustainable society.
Exclusive Interview with Andrea Debbane at Sustainability LIVE London 2024
Closed loop systems in automotive
JLR is making circularity a core pillar of its sustainability strategy by redesigning vehicles, materials and manufacturing processes to keep resources in use for longer. The company operates a Circularity Lab in Gaydon where it disassembles vehicles to identify barriers to reuse and recycling.
The lab feeds insights into future vehicle development and works with suppliers to create scalable closed-loop solutions. JLR's collaboration with Dow and Adient has delivered the automotive industry's first closed-loop recycled polyurethane seat foam.
The material returns from end-of-life vehicles into new luxury seats and reduces CO₂ emissions by more than 44kg per seat. JLR is also advancing circularity through its Cornerstone concept, which incorporates dozens of lower-impact components developed with more than 40 supply chain partners.
"As we are entering a critical phase in our
electrification journey
, JLR has at heart and aims to act as a responsible user of resources by enhancing product utility and longevity and maximising recycling and repurposing," says Andrea Debbane, Chief Sustainability Officer at JLR.
Paul Francis, Senior Manager Circularity at JLR, believes JLR can lead in advancing circularity across the automotive industry
Multi-party coordination across suppliers
Cornerstone components include recycled glass,
lower-emission
steel, repairable headlamps and speaker magnets made from 95% recycled materials. Paul Francis, Senior Manager Circularity at JLR, says the concept shows how JLR can lead in advancing circularity across the automotive industry.
"What we're achieving with Cornerstone shows how JLR can lead in advancing circularity across the automotive industry and the value of a coordinated, multi-party approach to deliver progress faster," says Paul. The company is reusing production equipment across manufacturing sites and expanding closed-loop aluminium recycling.
JLR is developing digital asset management systems to maximise reuse and designing future vehicles for easier repair, disassembly and material recovery. These changes strengthen both supply chain resilience and resource efficiency.
"It's not only the right thing to do, but it also improves profitability and increases supply chain resilience," says Andrea. "Through these initiatives,
JLR advocates that sustainable
choices are not always more expensive, they can help reduce costs and even become opportunities for the growth and development of our colleagues."

title: World Bank: East Asia’s Maritime Supply Chains At Risk
content:
World Bank: East Asia’s Maritime Supply Chains At Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
The regional maritime landscape faces mounting pressure from rising port congestion, ageing vessels, systemic safety deficiencies and the imperative to decarbonise operations. Credit: World Bank
World Bank report links port efficiency, safety and green fuels to resilient maritime supply chains across East Asia and the Pacific
Across East Asia and the Pacific, shipping functions as a core supply chain backbone, supporting between 16 and 18 million people whose livelihoods depend on global, regional and domestic trade flows.
Maritime transport ties together producers, consumers and energy systems, carrying bulk commodities, consumer goods and fuel across extensive archipelagos and busy trade corridors that feed manufacturing and retail networks.
interconnected logistics systems
now face growing strain from congested ports, ageing fleets, persistent safety gaps and the need to cut emissions across end‑to‑end operations.
For companies relying on the region, building resilient supply chains means combining higher efficiency with improved safety and long‑term environmental performance from quayside to open sea.
The World Bank explores this in its report Ports, Ships and Fuels: Maritime Efficiency, Safety and Sustainability in East Asia and Pacific, framing maritime policy choices through a supply chain lens.
Unlocking the benefits of fuel-efficient shipping represents a significant opportunity for both short-term and long-term economic and social gains. Credit: Jan Hoffmann/World Bank
Operational efficiency across trade corridors
The report identifies operational efficiency as the fastest way to improve performance along international supply chains that depend on ocean freight.
Ocean shipping is described as the most energy‑efficient transport mode, emitting between 11 and 17 grams of CO₂ per ton‑nautical mile, compared with 70 grams for heavy road freight and up to 515 grams for aviation, with direct implications for logistics cost and decarbonisation plans.
Between 2008 and 2024, global seaborne trade expanded by nearly 50%, yet energy use rose by only 5%, avoiding about 1.8 million barrels of oil a day and saving around US$60bn a year in fuel for transport networks.
Gateway ports such as Shanghai, China and Singapore are cited for rapid vessel turnaround, which stabilises
manufacturing supply chains
, while smaller archipelagic terminals struggle with slower cargo handling and longer waiting times that can disrupt feeder services and hinterland deliveries.
In developing economies across the region, port activity generates about 21.5 million tonnes of CO₂e each year, with ships responsible for 70 to 95% of air pollution inside port boundaries, affecting local communities and logistics workers.
“Maritime supply chains are the circulatory system of regional economies,” says Carlos Felipe Jaramillo, Vice President for East Asia and Pacific at The World Bank.
Carlos Felipe Jaramillo, Vice President for East Asia and Pacific, World Bank
“When they function well, businesses become more competitive, markets become more accessible and communities prosper.
“This report is a call to protect workers, strengthen maritime safety and seize the opportunities presented by a more efficient and sustainable maritime future.”
The World Bank report states that digital appointment systems and Just‑In‑Time arrivals can streamline vessel calls, cutting time at anchorage and reducing emissions around ports by up to 25%, which in turn supports more predictable supply chain schedules.
Safety, ageing assets and regulatory oversight
Port State Control regimes under the Tokyo Memorandum of Understanding carried out more than 32,000 inspections in 2024, leading to nearly 1,200 detentions for serious safety or environmental failures that can interrupt cargo flows.
The World Bank notes that East Asia and the Pacific supply more than 40% of the global seafarer workforce, making high‑quality training and strict crew certification central to reducing human error in complex maritime operations.
These human‑factor safeguards become even more important as operators introduce alternative fuels such as green methanol and green ammonia, which change fuel handling and emergency procedures along bunker supply chains.
Because these fuels are hazardous, with high toxicity and flammability, ports and shipowners must invest in gas‑detection systems, appropriate protective equipment and specialised emergency‑response training to manage operational risk.
Sustainable Mobility for All: It’s Not A Dream, It’s a Revolution
Fuel procurement and decarbonised supply chains
The report stresses that
long‑term sustainability
for maritime supply chains depends on shifting away from conventional fossil fuels, which still make up more than 99% of global marine fuel consumption.
Bunker fuel accounts for between 40 and 60% of vessel operating costs, so decisions on propulsion and fuel choice are highly sensitive to price signals and expectations about future fuel markets.
Liquefied Natural Gas currently dominates alternative fuel deployment, with more than 470 LNG‑fuelled vessels in service, but meeting net zero goals will require large‑scale adoption of green methanol and green ammonia across regional bunkering networks.
Extending efficiency improvements across all subsectors and scales of operation is essential to unlock broader productivity, safety and sustainability benefits.
Carlos Felipe Jaramillo, Vice President for East Asia and Pacific, World Bank.
Yet supply chain planning for these fuels is complicated by limited output: green methanol projects are producing only 0.034 million tonnes today, with a further 13.2 million tonnes still at feasibility stage, leaving shipowners uncertain about future availability.
Maritime operators also face competition from agriculture and chemical manufacturing for green ammonia, with these sectors consuming more than 181 million tonnes annually and able to absorb higher prices more easily than shipping.
The World Bank argues that clear regulatory direction and harmonised global standards are urgently needed to reduce risk for investors in dual‑fuel vessels, low‑carbon fuel production and new bunkering infrastructure in East Asia and the Pacific.
Governance, investment and supply chain impact
Re‑engineering maritime routes into
low‑carbon transport corridors
requires major capital commitments across ports, fleets and energy supply chains that serve regional and global trade.
For sustainability the maritime sector is at a decisive inflection point. Achieving long-term sustainability will depend on the availability, affordability and scalability of alternative fuels.
Carlos Felipe Jaramillo
Vice President for East Asia and Pacific, World Bank
Fuel production facilities add another large investment layer, with projected needs of US$310bn for green ammonia, US$81bn for green methanol and US$42bn for renewable Liquefied Natural Gas by 2040, extending maritime decarbonisation upstream into energy and industrial systems.
The report highlights public‑private partnerships and blended finance as key tools for de‑risking large projects such as port electrification and shore power installations, both of which help cut emissions around high‑volume logistics hubs.
Policy coordination is also essential, aligning
governance and procurement practices
across raw material suppliers, shipowners and terminal operators so that investment in greener technologies supports, rather than undermines, supply chain reliability.
The World Bank links these infrastructure upgrades to wider economic gains, noting that every additional one million tonnes of cargo handled through ports supports about 300 jobs in hinterland logistics, strengthening regional supply chain ecosystems.

title: BYD's electric kei car gets off to a strong start with over 5,000 orders in its first week
content:
Peter Johnson
| Jul 30 2026 - 7:01 am PT
electric kei car has already secured over 5,000 orders, more than half of its target by the end of 2026 in just one week.
BYD Racco secures more than 5,000 orders in one week
BYD is going where no foreign brand has gone before. The Chinese EV giant officially
launched Racco
in Japan on Tuesday, its first electric kei car specifically designed to crack open a market long dominated by domestic brands like Nissan, Honda, Toyota, and Suzuki.
The mini EV is reportedly already off to a promising start. According to
ChinaEVHome
, BYD’s electric kei car secured over 5,000 orders in one week after opening on July 21.
That’s already half of the initial 10,000 orders BYD aimed to achieve by the end of 2026. The feedback so far has been considerably stronger than for its previous vehicles.
Foot traffic in showrooms has also increased, with some dealers reportedly seeing over 200 customer visits. In its busiest showrooms, BYD has secured over 60 deposit orders in a single day.
BYD Racco (Source: BYD)
Interestingly, 70% of reservation holders are planning to trade in their existing kei car. The other 30% will add the Racco as a second vehicle.
Why are buyers interested? For one, BYD’s electric kei car is more efficient and, thanks to its electric powertrain, has lower maintenance costs. The Racco is also significantly more advanced as a software-defined vehicle (SDV), with software updates that can introduce new features, much like a smartphone.
BYD’s electric kei car starts at just ¥2,145,000, or about $13,000 in Japan. The base Racco 200 uses a 22.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles).
The higher-priced 300 Plus and Premium trims use a larger 35.84 kWh battery with a range up to 320 km (199 miles), which BYD said makes it the first kei EV in Japan to offer over 300 km.

title: China is starting to measure EV charging times in seconds, not minutes
content:
One of China’s newest EVs is also its fastest-charging, with the ability to fill its battery from 10-70% in 4 minutes and 22 seconds.
But that’s not the only recent announcement of a fast-charging battery that quotes how many seconds it takes to fill up, showing that the race for fast charging has entered a new era which treats seconds as the significant figure, rather than minutes.
Geely subsidiary Lynk & Co. recently launched its new 10 series EVs, complete with extreme fast charging speed. The cars are the first to use Geely’s “Golden Brick” battery, with more models coming soon at various Geely brands.
Meanwhile, BYD already has several vehicles out using its “Blade 2.0” battery, which also offers extremely fast charging.
These two batteries are both on the vanguard of a new generation of Chinese EVs that are making charging undeniably quick, at least if the right infrastructure is available.
Seconds are starting to matter in EV charging times
BYD says its Blade 2.0 can charge from 10-70% in 5 minutes. And Geely one-upped BYD by saying its Golden Brick can charge the same amount in 4 minutes and 22 seconds.
Another major battery manufacturer, CATL, recently showed off a commercial battery that can charge at an 8C rate, allowing a 20-80% charge in 6 minutes and 48 seconds. But that’s actually slow compared to its recent announcement of a consumer light-duty battery that can charge from 10-80% in just 3 minutes and 44 seconds.
CATL’s battery is not yet available in a vehicle, so it isn’t quite apples-to-apples when comparing to the BYD and Geely tech above, both of which are already on the road. But it’s not just a lab test of a cell, it’s a fully formed pack undergoing testing in real fast charging, and it’s from the world’s largest EV battery manufacturer, not some startup making stuff up in the hunt for venture capital.
CATL isn’t the only one with fast charging tech waiting in the wings. FAW group just announced a battery that can charge from 10-70% in 3 minutes and 41 seconds. That’s a slightly slower rate than CATL’s 10-80% in 3:44, but the difference there is mere seconds.
And so, we get to the point: the common thread among all of these is that each of them mention not just the number of minutes, but the number of seconds it takes to get a full charge. So China is now working with a different significant figure – seconds, not minutes.
Do such quick charge times matter?
The public has long felt that charging times are too long, and that EVs need to charge as fast as gas cars.
Never mind that that isn’t really true in practice – EV owners know that charging at home is even easier than going to gas stations, and on roadtrips, your car will often be ready by the time that you’re done with your stop. But the perception, among non-EV owners who are used to the anxiety-causing paradigm of being chained to gas stations, is that EV refueling needs to be substantially similar to the poor experience they’re used to.
There are still benefits. For example, higher power delivery means higher throughput, which means you can get more cars in and out of the same charging spot/station per day, which reduces land use needed. This can be important, particularly in urban environments, especially ones where people don’t have access to home charging.
So, regardless of whether these extremely fast charge times are necessary, the fact of the matter is that they already exist – at least in China.
What’s the best we have in the US?
Meanwhile, in the US, our fastest-charging vehicles have been the Hyundai/Kia E-GMP cars, which can charge from 10-80% in around 18 minutes on the right charger. That’s perfectly fine for roadtrips, especially since a driver will need to take a break every few hours while driving anyway.
But for people who rely on fast charging for all of their charging needs (seriously, try to find a way to charge at home if you can), even 18 minutes of sitting around in your car can feel like a long time. A 3 minute, 41 second charge seems a lot more palatable.
There is one vehicle coming out soon in the US which will be able to charge drastically faster than the E-GMP cars, the Mercedes AMG GT EV. That will be capable of about an 11 minute charge from 10-80% on a 600kW charger, which will put it well in the lead… but it’s going to be limited in production and cost well into the six figures. (In contrast, China’s fastest charging cars can be had for well under $30k)
But that one’s still measured in minutes. The difference between 11 minutes and 10 minutes and 30 seconds doesn’t seem like much, but the difference between 4 minutes and 3 minutes and 30 seconds seems a lot more significant. That’s why we didn’t start hearing seconds quoted in charging times until the minutes got down into single digits.
It’s not just the batteries, but the chargers, too
The question of 600kW chargers brings up another point – infrastructure rollout has been far faster inside China than outside it. Infrastructure is one of the major strengths of communist states, after all (for another example, see China’s rapid high speed rail network rollout).
BYD only announced its 1,500kW chargers earlier this year, and soon after, Geely rolled out 1,500kW chargers of its own. And then, just yesterday, state-owned Dongfeng announced its own 1,500kW charger, and says it’s working on even faster ones.
But it’s not just that the chargers exist, it’s that they’re already being deployed at a large scale. BYD plans to have 20,000 installed by year’s end, with several thousand already installed at this point. That sort of fast scaling simply doesn’t happen outside of China.
For example, it took about three years before the first “true” 500kW V4 Supercharger showed up in the wild (CEO Elon Musk’s idiotic move to fire the entire Supercharger team, thus causing complete chaos with contractors, couldn’t have helped).
Europe fares better with fast charging than the US, as there are several ~400kW charging units from companies like Alpitronic that are currently in operation, with 600kW stations rolling out this year.
But BYD isn’t content to wait in the overseas market, either. Europe recently got its first BYD flash chargers, and the company plans to roll out thousands of them in the next year. Perhaps BYD would roll out its flash charging system here, as it has in Europe, if the market were less hostile. But as of yet, it has no similar plans in the US (though Canada will get it soon.)
The US chose to have worse charging
It’s still rare to find even one or two 350kW chargers at a US charging station, let alone anything quicker.
President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act built programs to help accelerate the buildout of these chargers. But those programs have moved slower than they should, for several reasons both at the state and federal level.
One of those reasons is intentional, held back by the republican party, mostly at the federal level.
The reality TV contestant squatting in the Department of Transportation spent most of last year illegally trying to pause disbursement of funds, then being stopped by court. In addition, the joint office that Biden created to increase government collaboration and efficiency was dismantled, making DoT and DoE less efficient.
Even after being stopped by court, DoT has tried to put up more roadblocks by refusing funding to chargers with any Chinese components (the Biden-era regulation required a 55% US components, rather than 100%).
Not only is this impossible because the US simply doesn’t make all the parts needed for EV chargers, it also restricts America from having access to the best chargers available (as we learned above are being made by Chinese companies), and is done in the context of republicans shipping EV jobs to China by canceling Biden-era programs that had led to a renaissance in US manufacturing.
Top comment by WhereIsTheElectricMiata?
The growing number of tech bans on whole classes of products like robots (including Roombas) and routers is also keeping us from having nice things. Of course they claim it’s for security and to build our manufacturing base, and then they arbitrarily give waivers without regard for any security reassurances or plans for investments. And there is no effort to remediate the actual security and privacy issues that current products in our homes have.
All of this happened after the party’s candidate asked for and got bribes from the oil industry (in his campaign to run for an office he is Constitutionally barred from holding), so it’s no wonder why there have been so many attacks on the industry promising a better future than oil.
So, here, in the land of plenty, rather than competing to be the best of the best and working to onshore manufacturing of the best products out there, America is pushing those products away, and letting the rest of the world enjoy these cool things that we are deprived of (and China is profitinf from providing them to the world).
Instead, we wallow alone in the pollution forced on us as a result of those oil company bribes, subject to the whims of a senile dictator with no concept of how geopolitics (or anything) works, losing an industry we could have been a player in, and refusing to join the world in improving the fates of our citizens.

title: Tesla hits 10 million vehicles — but its EV growth has stalled
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 30 2026 - 6:36 am PT
Tesla has built its 10 millionth vehicle, the company announced this week. Ten million all-electric cars is a real milestone, and no other automaker has done it.
But it’s arriving later than Tesla once promised, and the company is now building well under the capacity it already has.
The 50% growth that just stopped
For years, Tesla guided investors toward roughly 50% average annual growth in production and deliveries. Elon Musk repeated that target on call after call. And for a while, the numbers backed it up.
Then it stopped. Tesla peaked at 1.81 million deliveries in 2023. In 2024, it posted
its first-ever annual decline
, at about 1.79 million. In 2025, deliveries fell again to 1,636,129, down 9% year over year. That’s two straight years of decline, and 2026 is so far not much better.
So the 10 millionth car is an incredible milestone for Tesla, and those involved should be proud, but it should have happened a long time ago. It was announced today:
Produced our 10 millionth Tesla globally at Fremont Factory this week!
Only 6 years ago, Fremont Factory made our 1 millionth vehicle
Tesla has an explanation for the delay. In its
first-quarter 2024 shareholder update
, the company said it was “currently between two major growth waves.” The first wave was the Model 3 and Model Y. The second was supposed to be a cheaper next-generation vehicle.
It’s now more than two years later. The second wave still isn’t here.
Tesla is running its factories well below capacity
Here’s the part that doesn’t get talked about enough. By Tesla’s own accounting, it has already built the factory capacity for a much bigger car company than the one it’s running.
Tesla’s own installed annual manufacturing capacity, from its latest figures:
Add up the vehicle lines listed at “Production” status and Tesla claims more than 2.375 million units of annual capacity: over 950,000 in Shanghai, more than 550,000 in Fremont, over 375,000 in Berlin, and 250,000 Model Y plus 125,000 Cybertruck and 125,000 Cybercab in Texas.
Now compare that to what Tesla is actually building. In
, Tesla produced 451,758 vehicles and delivered 480,126. At that quarterly rate, Tesla is on pace for roughly 1.8 million vehicles this year. That’s more than half a million units short of what its own plants can produce.
And demand is running below even that. Tesla delivered 1.636 million cars in 2025 while it had capacity for well over 2 million. The company isn’t supply-constrained. It’s demand-constrained, and it’s underutilizing manufacturing assets it spent billions to build.
The lineup problem
The reason is simple. The Model 3 and Model Y are the two best-selling EVs in the world, but they’ve been on sale since 2017 and 2020. The Cybertruck flopped. The Cybercab and Semi are still ramping. The Roadster is stuck in “design development,” where it has been for years.
Meanwhile, Tesla has pointed its energy and attention at robotaxis and Optimus. Its
robotaxi fleet is actually shrinking
, not growing, and
Optimus keeps slipping
. Neither sells a single extra car.
Electrek’s Take
Ten million all-electric vehicles is a genuinely great milestone, and Tesla deserves credit for it. No legacy automaker is close. Tesla did more than anyone to prove EVs could be built at scale and sell in the millions, and 10 million cars carrying its badge is the receipt.
But this milestone is also a reminder that Tesla’s EV business has flatlined. The growth story that carried the stock for a decade ended in 2023, and
we’ve been saying the growth story is dead
for a while now. Two straight years of falling deliveries, on a lineup that’s mostly the same cars Tesla was selling five years ago, and factories running with hundreds of thousands of units of slack. That’s not a pause between two growth waves. That’s a company that stopped investing in the next EV and bet the future on robots and robotaxis instead.
My problem with it is simple: it was avoidable. Elon Musk lost his touch and pushed Tesla all-in on autonomy and robotics too early. The bets haven’t paid off, and there’s a chance they never will, as Musk’s approach to autonomy is getting surpassed by competition.

title: Plug-in port: Brazilian Port of Santos electrifies DP World terminal
content:
Electric Semi Truck
Electric Heavy Machinery
Jo Borrás
| Jul 30 2026 - 5:06 am PT
Jeddah Terminal, by DP World.
DP World is electrifying its port fleet at the Brazilian Port of Santos with 15 battery-electric terminal trucks and three electric reach stackers in a move that marks another key step toward clean freight handling at one of Latin America’s busiest container ports.
The deployment of the new electric equipment assets are part of DP World’s 1.6 billion Real (BRL) expansion at its Santos terminal, which will allow the company to handle more than 2 million twenty-foot equivalent container units (TEUs) annually by 2028.
The investment is the first phase of a broader terminal modernization initiative from DP World that will see the deployment of a total of 44 electric terminal tractors,
three electric reach stackers
four new electric quay cranes
, and fifteen 40-ton class rubber-tired gantry cranes (RTGs) already scheduled for delivery before the end of 2027.
“We continue to invest in infrastructure and equipment that enables us to deliver greater capacity, reliability, efficiency and sustainability for our customers,”
said Fabio Siccherino
, CEO of DP World Brazil. “These new electric vehicles strengthen our operations today while supporting increasing trade volumes and the long-term growth of Brazil’s trade.”
Electric terminal tractors at Callao
Terberg electric terminal tractors, by DP World.
DP World’s press release didn’t specify what kind of terminal tractors they’re deploying at Santos, the company has an established relationship with Dutch terminal truck brand Terberg, which has delivered a fleet of 20 Terberg YT203-EV yard hostlers at DP World’s Callao terminal in Peru, and another few dozen at its London Gateway site.
The YT203-EV packs a 236 kWh capacity battery pack with enough juice to run up to 20 hours a day at the Callao site (above),
averaging nearly 12 hours of operation on a single charge
Between January and April of 2026, diesel consumption declined 29.2% compared with the 2024 average, and is expected to reduce carbon emissions by more than 500 tons –
a huge gain in sustainability that underscores both the financial
and environmental impacts of investing in port modernization.

title: Türkiye adds 2.1 GW of solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Türkiye’s solar additions from the first half of the year take total capacity to around 26.9 GW. The number of solar plants in the country now exceeds 41,000, up from around 37,600 at the start of the year.
Patrick Jowett
30 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Image: Michael Jerrard/Unsplash
added 2.1 GW of new solar capacity during the first half of 2026, according to figures from energy think tank Ember.
The figure takes the country’s cumulative capacity to around 26.9 GW when adding to
last year’s deployment figures
. By the end of June, the number of solar plants in Türkiye had exceeded 41,000, up from around 37,600 at the beginning of the year.
This year’s growth helped solar record its highest-ever monthly share of electricity generation in Türkiye last month. Data from the country’s energy exchange company EPİAŞ shows solar accounted for 16.5% of electricity generation in June, setting a new all-time monthly record and surpassing the previous record of 16.1% in June 2025. Solar generation reached approximately 5 TWh during June, another all-time high.
Bahadır Sercan Gümüş, energy analyst for Ember, told
pv magazine
1.8 GW of this year’s additions so far come from unlicensed power plants. Such projects, designed for self-consumption up to a 5 MW, make up the majority of Türkiye’s operational solar fleet.
“Although Türkiye has a substantial pipeline of licensed projects, including [government] tenders and storage-integrated plants, commissioning has remained slower than expected,” Gümüş explained. “I believe self-consumption projects will remain the main growth driver for the rest of the year, as they continue to be commissioned much faster than licensed projects. And at this stage, I expect the current pace to continue through the remainder of the year.”
Gümüş believes the most significant regulatory development in Türkiye during the first half of the year was the transition from monthly netting to hourly netting for self-consumption plants.
“While this is expected to reduce project revenues to some extent, the impact should be relatively limited,” he explained. “It is also worth noting that residential consumers were exempt from the new regulation, which applies only to commercial and industrial consumers.”
Gümüş added that as distributed generation expands, grid management is becoming increasingly important, particularly as Türkiye introduced regulations allowing TEİAŞ to curtail generation from unlicensed plants during periods of excess supply.
“Although this mechanism has rarely been used so far, I expect curtailment to become a more common balancing tool, particularly during periods of low demand and high renewable output,” Gümüş told
pv magazine
. “This will be an important indicator to monitor in the coming years.”
Türkiye’s first storage-integrated solar plant began commercial operations during the first half of 2026, Gümüş continued, reaching 260 MW.
Storage reached a monthly charge-discharge volume of approximately 14 GWh in June which corresponds to about 0.05% of monthly consumption. Gümüş said that while storage has not yet reached a level that would impact the market, he expects Türkiye’s huge project stock to be commissioned gradually over the coming years, albeit at a slow pace.
“If the rollout of storage-integrated projects accelerates, Türkiye could match, or even exceed, last year’s installation levels, although we have not yet seen that acceleration,” he said.
The Turkish government is continuing to tender large-scale renewable programs, most recently with plans to procure
900 MW of solar
and 1.5 GW of wind under its next Renewable Energy Resource Area (YEKA) program in October.
Gümüş told
pv magazine
it is understood the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources may announce an increase to its 120 GW solar and wind target for 2035 during COP31, scheduled to take place in Ankara in November.
“Achieving this target would require annual additions of more than 8 GW of solar and wind capacity,” Gümüş added. “At the moment, Türkiye is still some distance from sustaining that level of deployment.”

title: Indonesia signals start of 100 GW solar initiative - pv magazine Global

Indonesia’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, says a groundbreaking ceremony will soon take place for the first phase of the country’s flagship 100 GW solar program.

Bahlil Lahadalia | Image: Indonesia’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources
Indonesia’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, has said the first phase of a 100 GW solar power project will begin in the near future.
Speaking to press earlier this week, Lahadalia said the first phase of the project has been approved for implementation and will soon enter construction with the launch of the first groundbreaking ceremony.
Indonesia’s plan to deploy 100 GW of solar was first announced in
August 2025
. The initiative is targeting the installation of 80 GW of decentralized, small-scale solar systems with accompanying battery energy storage systems to be deployed across 80,000 villages, alongside 20 GW of centralized solar.
In a statement sent to
pv magazine
, Fabby Tumiwa, Chief Executive Officer of the Jakarta-based the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), said the think tank welcomes the step forward in advancing the 100 GW development plan.
Tumiwa called on the government to position the initiative within a comprehensive and just transformation of Indonesia’s energy system, with the country’s existing Village Electrification Program, known as Lisdes, serving as an integral component.
The Lisdes program is a government initiative bringing reliable electricity to remote, disadvantaged and outermost regions of Indonesia. According to Lahadalia’s update earlier this week, the program has already reached more than 1,400 villages across Indonesia from around 11,000 without electricity.
“Village electrification should no longer be viewed merely as a means of improving electrification ratio statistics. Instead, it should aim to provide reliable and adequate energy access for all Indonesians while fostering the productive use of energy to stimulate local economic development,” Tumiwa said.
“By integrating the Village Electrification Program into the 100 GW Solar Program based on local renewable energy potential, the government will not only pursue solar generation capacity targets but also promote rural economic growth, accelerate energy democratization, and deliver a just energy transition that reaches even the most remote communities across the Indonesian archipelago.”
Earlier this year, IESR released a report exploring how Indonesia can
mobilize its 100 GW solar target
. It found reaching the goal will require an estimated $140-210 billion through the first phase investment as it called for support from financial institutions, green financing mechanisms and the private sector. It also warned against trying to adopt a one-size-fits all approach to electrifying the 80,000 villages.

content:

Colombia’s Ministry of Mines and Energy awarded contracts for around 270 MW of new solar tied to 100 MW of battery energy storage in the first round of its long-term clean energy auction. The 15-year contracts begin supplying electricity in 2030.
Luis Ini
30 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Flavia Carpio/Unsplash
Colombia’s Ministry of Mines and Energy has awarded contracts for around 270 MW of new solar tied to 100 MW of battery energy storage in the first round of its long-term clean energy auction.
The ministry says the auction awarded 390 MWh per day under the hybrid product, which combines solar photovoltaic generation with battery energy storage. The contracts require electricity delivery in two time blocks: from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., primarily from solar generation, and from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m., when batteries shift solar output into the evening peak.
The awarded capacity increases Colombia’s installed battery storage capacity by about 1,000%, the ministry added, providing enough contracted energy to meet peak-hour demand from more than 67,000 households.
The auction cleared at COP 315.87 ($0.099)/kWh. The ministry said the price is less than 30% of electricity prices that can occur in the spot market during drought periods.
“The results obtained on this first day of the auction mark a milestone for the country’s just energy transition,” said Minister of Mines and Energy Edwin Palma. “Multiplying energy storage capacity and incorporating more solar generation into the energy mix reaffirms the government’s commitment to decarbonization and electricity system reliability.”
The contracts have a 15-year term, with supply obligations beginning Jan. 1, 2030. The auction uses a pay-as-contracted structure, with sellers bidding prices in Colombian pesos per kilowatt-hour, plus the applicable reliability charge component.
A second auction round took place yesterday (July 29), covering standalone solar photovoltaic projects and new or existing plants equipped with battery storage to supply electricity between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m.
Final audited results are expected after all auction stages conclude later today (July 30).

Jordan’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources has announced the completion of the first phase of a project to install solar-powered water heating systems at hospitals across the country.

The first phase of the project was implemented by Noor Solar Energy following
a tender
held in October last year. The project is aiming to install solar water heating systems in 33 hospitals in total across three phases at a total cost of JOD 3.2 million ($4.5 million).
Once completed, the project is expected to provide around 217,000 litres of hot water daily across the hospitals, while achieving annual financial savings estimated at over JOD 266,000.
The project is administered by the Jordan Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Fund (JREEEF) and has been supported by the Italian government.
During a site visit of one of the installations, JREEEF executive director, Rasmi Hamza, explained that the project falls within the framework of the fund’s efforts to enhance energy efficiency in the health sector by providing a sustainable and safe source of hot water.
Hamza said the project also contributes to reducing the consumption of traditional fuels, while also reducing operating costs and improving the quality of health services provided to citizens.
Jordan’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 2,195 MW by the end of the last year, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the same figure reported at the end of the year prior.

content:

Uruguay is planning to deploy an additional 500 MW of new renewables before the end of the current administration in February 2030. The plan includes four new solar projects, two of which have already been identified.
Luis Ini
30 Jul 2026

Markets & Policy
Americas
Utility-scale

Uruguay’s Minister of Industry, Energy and Mining, Fernanda Cardona, has said the government plans to add 500 MW of new renewable capacity before the end of the current administration in February 2030, with an emphasis on photovoltaic energy.
Cardona announced the intention during the opening of the XII Latin American Renewable Energy Congress, organized by the Uruguayan Renewable Energy Association on July 28 and 29 at the Technological Laboratory of Uruguay in Montevideo, the country’s capital.
The 500 MW target includes four solar plants and the advancement of hybridization initiatives, although no concrete battery storage projects have yet been presented.
“In recent years, we have fallen behind in terms of adding new generation capacity,” Cardona stated. She explained that expanding renewable energy is a key component of the government’s energy policy and must prepare the system for projects that will demand a more competitive, reliable, and sustainable supply.
Two of the four plants have already been identified
Cardona indicated that the four solar power plants will be located in different departments across the country, with the first one being installed in Cerro Largo, northern Uruguay. This project is the Melo Photovoltaic Solar Park, previously presented by the state-owned electric company UTE,
which began construction in April
The Melo plant will have an installed capacity of 100 MWp and a nominal capacity of 75 MW at its point of connection. The project includes approximately 140,000 solar modules with trackers, an investment of over $75 million, and a 150 kV connection via the Melo B substation. UTE estimates that it will be able to supply the equivalent of approximately 65,000 homes.
The second project identified so far is a 30 MW photovoltaic plant that UTE initially planned to build in the department of Durazno but will be moved to the northwestern department of Río Negro following legal challenges and administrative issues that arose regarding the original site.
UTE indicated in May that the Río Negro project already had environmental permits and that it expected to begin contracting and construction in the short term
. The company maintains its intention to later develop another solar power plant in Baygorria.
The 30 MW initiative had also been presented with
a financing scheme open to small investors, with contributions starting at $200
Minister Cardona did not provide details about the other two solar facilities planned, nor did she specify what proportion of the total 500 MW five-year project will correspond to photovoltaic generation.
Uruguay ended 2025 with 339 MW of installed and connected solar photovoltaic capacity, compared to 336 MW at the end of 2024, according to the most recent statistics from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).
The country has a high renewable energy share, averaging around 97% of electricity generation, led by hydro and wind power. Cardona stated that this does not eliminate the need to expand the energy mix with new projects.
“It would be a mistake to think the job is done,” she said, linking new projects to increased demand, the electrification of transportation and industrial development.

Berlin-headquartered solar company Enpal is closing its sales office in Hamburg. A company spokesperson confirmed to

Shortly after news of the closure emerged, Philipp Schröder, founder of 1Komma5°, responded on LinkedIn. The company is headquartered in Hamburg and is one of Enpal’s main competitors for customers looking to install photovoltaic systems, battery storage, heat pumps, EV chargers, and intelligent energy management systems.
Schröder announced that he intended to make job offers to Enpal’s Hamburg employees in an effort to preserve as many positions as possible. “No matter how different our strategy, business model and culture may be, the goal is the same,” Schröder wrote on LinkedIn.
Third public securitization completed
On Wednesday, Enpal announced the successful completion of a third public securitisation of residential photovoltaic systems and heat pumps with M&G Investments. The issuance had a total volume of €367 million.
The asset-backed securities (ABS) transaction was based on a mixed portfolio of around 11,500 loans provided to German homeowners for photovoltaic systems and heat pumps. According to the company, 99% of the invested capital came from Europe, although Enpal also said it is seeing growing interest from US investors.

title: Chinese researchers build 29.71% perovskite-CIGS tandem solar cell based on sulfide - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in China developed a four-terminal perovskite/CIGS tandem solar cell using bis(2-pyridylmethyl) sulfide (2PyS) coordination engineering to improve wide-bandgap perovskite stability by suppressing defects, halide migration, and phase segregation.
Emiliano Bellini
30 Jul 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Schematic of the tandem solar cell | Image: Chinese Academy of Science, IOPScience, CC BY 4.0
Researchers from the
Chinese Academy of Sciences
(CAS) have developed a tandem solar cell based on a top perovskite solar cell and a bottom device relying on copper, indium, gallium and selenium (CIGS) using a coordination-engineering approach designed to improve the stability of the wide-bandgap perovskite material.
They used, in particular, an organic sulfur-containing compound known as bis(2-pyridylmethyl) sulfide (2PyS) to fine-tune the local coordination environment of lead (Pb) ions within the perovskite layer. This strategy helped limit defect formation, suppress halide ion migration, and reduce photoinduced phase segregation, addressing key stability challenges in wide-bandgap perovskite absorbers.
“A key origin of this instability is the presence of undercoordinated Pb defects and associated halide vacancies,” they explained. “These defects not only act as recombination centers but also disturb the local lattice environment and provide pathways for halide ion migration. Conventional post-treatment passivation strategies can reduce some defects after crystallization, but they often offer limited control over defect formation during the film growth process. As a result, photoinduced halide segregation remains difficult to suppress during long-term device operation.”
The top perovskite cell was built with an indium tin oxide (ITO) front electrode, a nickel oxide (NiOx) hole transport layer, a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) interfacial layer, a perovskite light-absorbing layer, a C60 fullerene electron transport layer, a tin oxide (SnO₂) buffer layer, an indium tin oxide (ITO) transparent electrode, and a silver (Ag) metal contact.
The subcell consisted of a molybdenum (Mo) rear electrode for charge collection, a CIGS absorber optimized for long-wavelength light harvesting, a cadmium sulfide (CdS) buffer layer for interface passivation, and zinc oxide-based window layers comprising intrinsic zinc oxide (i-ZnO) and aluminum-doped zinc oxide (Al:ZnO) for electron transport and transparent front contact formation.
The standalone CIGS bottom cell demonstrated a power conversion efficiency of 19.65% under full-spectrum illumination. When operated beneath the semi-transparent perovskite top cell, the available incident light was reduced due to spectral filtering, leading to a decrease in the subcell efficiency to 7.5%. As for the top cell, it achieved an efficiency 22.21%, while in a four-terminal (4T) tandem configuration, the integrated tandem device reached an overall efficiency of 29.71%. The devices were also found to retain more than 91% of their initial efficiency after 2000 hours of continuous operation.
This performance is described by the scientists as among the highest efficiencies reported for perovskite/CIGS four-terminal tandem solar cells to date. They also explained that 2PyS binds more strongly to lead iodide (PbI₂) than commonly used solvents such as dimethylformamide (DMF) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). This stronger interaction enables 2PyS to more effectively regulate the coordination environment of Pb ions during perovskite formation, thereby influencing the crystallization process.
“Moreover, in situ photoluminescence measurements further revealed that 2PyS modulates crystallization kinetics, suppresses rapid nucleation, and promotes more homogeneous film growth,” the research team concluded. “As a result, the modified perovskite films exhibit improved optoelectronic properties, reduced non-radiative recombination, enhanced structural integrity, and stronger phase stability under coupled illumination and thermal stress.”
The new cell concept was presented in “
Coordination-regulated defect suppression enables stable wide-bandgap perovskites for efficient perovskite/CIGS tandem solar cells
,” published in
IPOScience
